title: We found 4 stable customer personas — commit next quarter's budget by persona?

scenario.role: You're the marketing analyst at Millbrook
scenario.situation: Owen, the CMO, ran k-means (k=4, chosen from an elbow plot) on engagement_score and value_score, got 4 clean-looking personas, and named them for the media plan. He wants to lock in next quarter's ad budget split by persona size before the planning deadline — and asked you to just confirm the persona sizes are right.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "We ran the clustering and found 4 real personas. Let's commit next quarter's ad budget split to match their sizes — this is settled, just confirm the numbers."
scenario.question: Are these 4 personas actually stable — the same clustering you'd get if you re-ran it tomorrow — or did one particular run just happen to draw those boundaries? Check whether the persona assignment survives a re-run before budget gets locked to it.

columns.name: cluster_run1
columns.description: K-means(k=4) cluster label from the first run, fit on engagement_score/value_score (standardized)

columns.name: cluster_run2
columns.description: K-means(k=4) cluster label from a second run — same data, same k, only the random initialization differs (like re-running the job on a different day without a pinned seed). Labels are pre-matched to run1's numbering for comparison.

guidingQuestions: What share of customers have the same cluster_run1 and cluster_run2? (Labels are already matched, so a direct equality check is valid.)
For customers who DID change cluster between runs, where do they sit in engagement_score/value_score space — near the middle of the pack, or out at the extremes?
Plot (or describe) engagement_score vs. value_score. Do you see 4 visually distinct, well-separated groups, or more of a continuous cloud?
If you had to guess how many *real* separated groups are in this data by eye, would you say 4?
If Owen locks next quarter's ad budget to the 4 persona sizes from cluster_run1, and the real underlying data hasn't changed at all — what happens when someone re-runs the same clustering next month?
suggestedApproach: Compute the share of customers where cluster_run1 == cluster_run2 — this is the reproducibility rate.
Isolate the customers who switched clusters and check where they sit relative to the boundary between clusters — likely clustered near cluster boundaries, not randomly scattered.
Visualize (or bucket) engagement_score against value_score and look for whether 4 genuinely separated blobs exist, or one continuous, overlapping cloud.
Consider what k actually fits: does the data support a cleaner, smaller number of groups than 4?
State the real risk in business terms: an ad-budget split locked to cluster sizes that reshuffle ~15% of customers on a re-run with the exact same underlying population.

teachingNote.naiveRead: K-means ran, 4 clusters came out, they got named, and the sizes look final enough to lock next quarter's budget split against.
teachingNote.theTrap: K-means is a local-search algorithm: it starts from a random set of initial cluster centers and converges to whichever partition is nearest that starting point, not necessarily the one globally best partition. When the underlying data doesn't have 4 cleanly separated groups — here, it's really closer to 2 broad, overlapping groups, and k=4 was chosen from an elbow-plot ritual rather than genuine structure — the two "extra" clusters get carved out of that continuous cloud roughly wherever the random initialization happens to land. Re-run the exact same clustering on the exact same data, with only the random seed different, and 15% of customers land in a different cluster than before. The clusters aren't measuring something real and stable about each customer; a meaningful chunk of the "persona" label is just which random start the algorithm happened to get.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Before locking a budget split to cluster sizes, check reproducibility: re-run the clustering (different seed, same data) and measure how many customers keep the same cluster. Here, only 85% do (adjusted Rand index ≈ 0.68 between the two runs) — genuine instability, not noise you can ignore. The honest move is either to stabilize the clustering (many more random restarts and take a consensus/majority-vote label, or fit on standardized data with a k chosen by a stability-aware method rather than a single elbow plot) or, more simply, to check whether the data actually supports 4 groups at all — here it doesn't; the real structure is closer to 2 broad segments. Tell Owen: don't lock next quarter's budget to a 4-way split that a different Tuesday's random seed would have drawn differently. Either stabilize the method or reduce to the segment count the data actually supports.
howToGetThere: Re-run k-means(k=4) on the identical dataset with only the random seed changed; match cluster labels between the two runs by maximum overlap (Hungarian algorithm).
Compute the share of customers with the same matched cluster in both runs: ≈ 85% — meaning 15% reshuffle.
Compute the adjusted Rand index between the two runs' labels: ≈ 0.68 — meaningfully below 1.0, confirming real instability, not just label-numbering noise.
Visualize engagement_score vs. value_score: the data forms one broad, overlapping cloud rather than 4 visually separated blobs.
Conclude: k=4 doesn't reflect genuine structure in this data; treat cluster identity here as unstable rather than a fixed customer trait.

numbers.label: Customers with the same cluster across two re-runs
Customers reassigned to a different cluster
Adjusted Rand index between the two runs
Genuinely separated groups visible in the data

teachingNote.lesson: K-means always returns an answer, even when the data doesn't have the number of clean, separated groups you asked for — and that answer can depend heavily on the random starting point rather than on real structure. Before treating a clustering result as a stable customer attribute (worth budget, campaigns, or roadmap decisions), re-run it and measure agreement. If the same data produces meaningfully different clusters from run to run, the instability is telling you something important: either stabilize the method (more restarts, consensus clustering) or reduce k to the number of groups the data actually supports.
